utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Registrar, could you please call the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-66-R77, the Prosecutor versus Beqa Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now turning to the Prosecution. I believe that we will be hearing the last witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And who is this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Jonathan Sutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. How long do you think his -- how long do you think your examination-in-chief will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Approximately 60 minutes to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address the Bench very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: This is on an administrative matter. Our original witness list had seven witnesses, including one who was -- is a law enforcement officer from the town where B1 had located and who oversaw the recording of the October 6 call. When we reached an agreement with Defence counsel stipulating to the authenticity and admissibility of that exhibit, we withdrew her from the list. After this witness finishes we are going to be moving, asking the Court to admit all of the exhibits based on the stipulation. If the Court would like to have that witness come up from that country to testify, because we do not have the Court order in hand for that call, we can have that witness come and make that testimony, but since we had a stipulation as to its admissibility and authenticity, in order to save time and be efficient I withdrew her. But I'm happy to put her back on the list and get her up next week. I do have a court order that is also on the witness list which I can tender. I was planning not to because of the stipulation. I also have the written stipulation, signed stipulation from the Defence that I would tender today, but I would like some direction from the Court as to whether or not you want that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for that explanation. The Trial Chamber will consider this request and we'll inform you of our decision as soon as possible, but if Defence counsel has no objections I do not really believe it will be necessary to call the witness. But we will render a decision and you will be informed in due course of the Chamber's decision. Having said that, Mr. Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please. Is there anything else you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Before you testify, I would like you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please sit down. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Good morning. Could we have your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: My name is Jonathan Peter Sutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I'm an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: How long have you had this position?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Since 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What did you do before that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Prior to that, from 1986 to 2000 I was a police officer in the United Kingdom, having been a detective since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Have you had the occasion to speak with the accused, Beqa Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I first spoke to him on the 19th of October last year, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: At his home address in Shtime, in the region of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Can you -- one moment. What was the purpose of your going to this town to speak with the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Information had been received by the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the defendant and his contact with witnesses in another case before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of the pseudonyms in this case for the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: -- or do I need to refresh your recollection off the record?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No. I'm aware. I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you work with another investigator in this case?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: In Kosovo, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: When you speak about the incidents that led up to your occasion to meet with the accused, how did you learn of the facts that you were to discuss with the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Most if not all of the information was passed to me by Howard Tucker, another investigator, based in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. At this point I'm going to ask if you can go into the incidents that led up to your interviewing the accused. I'll start with can you describe the behaviour or alleged behaviour that you were going to interview him about.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: There had been a number of telephone calls made to a witness who had been relocated from the region of Kosovo, whereby that person was being asked not to testify in the case before the Tribunal. The content of those telephone conversations had been recorded, and upon analysis of those transcripts of the recordings, it seemed on the face of it that the person using the telephone and speaking to the witness could be committing offences under the Statute of the Tribunal. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Let me just ask a question to confirm. You mentioned the witness. Can you give us the pseudonym for this witness, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Can you now go into detail about the offences that may have been committed.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Specifically, interfering with witnesses, contempt of the Tribunal. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Go ahead and take a minute if you need to.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, it's okay. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to review the wire-tapped conversations before you spoke with the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, I didn't review the conversations, but I did have meetings, mainly telephone conversations, with colleagues concerning the content of the wire-tapped conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And they prepared you for the interview with the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Do you remember in detail these conversations with the investigator, Howard Tucker?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, not in detail. I can obviously recall the basic content of the conversations, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Let's go to October 19th, when you went to the accused's house. How did you proceed at that point?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: The intention was at that time just to make an arrangement for an interview with the accused. I went with an interpreter from the Tribunal who was permanently based in Kosovo. Went to the accused's house and -- I'm sorry, I'm going to have to take another drink of water. Went to the accused's house, where I identified myself to the accused and -- thank you. I was invited in to speak to him. In his home, I fully introduced myself, explained why I wanted to speak to him, that we had reason to believe that he may have been involved in actions that could constitute an offence under the Statute of the Tribunal and that it was my intention to interview him, not at his home address but in the ICTY offices in Pristina. I further informed him at that time that if necessary, he could have somebody present during the interview, legal representation, and if he didn't have a lawyer, we would arrange to have one present for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: At that point, how did the accused respond?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: He said that he'd only been in contact with one witness, or words to that effect, at which point I interrupted him and cautioned him telling him that he didn't have to say anything but anything that he did say at that point would be used in evidence. Again he continued saying that -- words to the effect of he had spoken to somebody and if they wanted to give evidence, that was a matter for them. I didn't go into detail with him at this point because I wasn't in a position to electronically record the conversation, and it was my intention to conduct the interview not at his home address. So we made an arrangement to meet two days later at the Pristina field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did he mention the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, he didn't, not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. What happened with the arrangements? Can you specify what the arrangements were?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: He later called to say that he didn't want to meet two days later at the field office, and that it was his intention not to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What did you do at that point?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: This information was passed to my colleagues here in The Hague, and subsequently a suspect summons was issued by the Prosecutor concerning the accused in order that we could then take further steps to ensure an interview took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What steps did you then take?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Later that day, I went back to his home address. I'd previously been introduced to him. I presented him, served him with the summons, and -- excuse me. He agreed to come with me to the offices in Pristina, some 20, 30 minutes away by car. And we subsequently conducted an interview later that night, just myself, an interpreter and Mr. Beqaj who had at that time declined the offer of legal representation during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you record the interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: On this occasion, yes. The interview was tape recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Who did the tape recording?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: I'm going to ask some foundational questions regarding the tape recording, in terms of its admissibility. Were you familiar with the machine you used to record the interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you test it before you taped the interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, as always, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you listen to the tape after the interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did it accurately reflect the interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Do you know if the accused received a copy of the tape?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, a copy would have been served, yes, although not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: How did the interview proceed?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: The interview itself actually didn't really centre on any of the telephone intercepts, the reason being at that stage was that it was the OTP's decision, or the investigation's decision, that we wouldn't disclose that element. So the interview centred on the accused's knowledge of people giving evidence in a specific case before the Tribunal and his contact with anybody of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did the accused in general admit that he had any knowledge of witnesses in the case or -- let me stop there. Any knowledge of witnesses in the case?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No. The interview was essentially a number of denials concerning knowledge of people involved in the case, the only exceptions being that the elements that were known generally throughout Kosovo as a result of media coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: So at this point, you had information about specific calls from the wire-taps. And did he verify or deny information that you had from these wire-taps?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, he did not, no. Well, sorry, there were denials. There was no verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. Based on the interview, what happened?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Based on that interview, a provisional request for arrest was issued by the Prosecutor under Article 40 of the Tribunal, and -- under the Statute, sorry. And he was subsequently taken into custody by the UNMIK police, the UN police in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to interview him again after the October 19th interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I interviewed him two days later, this time with legal representation, which I subsequently arranged for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What was the name of the legal representative?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: It was a man by the name of Azem Vllasi, who is a Kosovo-based -- Kosovo Albanian lawyer, who was asked by name actually by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Who else was present at this interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: There was myself, Mr. Pekka Havarinen, who is a former investigator for the Tribunal, and Mr. Artan Grubi, who is the Tribunal interpreter who had been used previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: And the accused, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you record this interview?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Again, using the same equipment, in fact. The interview was recorded throughout and the same conditions applied. The equipment was tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: You tested it beforehand and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I would like to ask that Exhibits 13 and 14, which are the interview transcripts, be admitted into evidence based on the foundation laid by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that we said we would be rendering a decision with regard to all the documents that the Prosecution wants to tender into evidence. We will mark them for identification and the decision will be rendered at a subsequent date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to know whether Defence counsel objects to these documents being tendered into evidence. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Registrar, could you mark these exhibits for identification, mark them with the abbreviation MFI.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 13, Your Honours, will be P9 MFI and number 14 will be P10 MFI. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dominguez, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sutch, I'd like to play a clip from the second interview, the October 21st interview, and ask a few questions. So by leave of the Court we are going to play a clip. So if we can have the audio/video systems fired up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: You told us on Tuesday that you knew nobody that is a witness or has ever expressed their willingness to testify at the Tribunal in the Limaj trial. "BB: It is true I didn't --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Let me start by asking you if you can identify the voices in this audio clip.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: The first voice is mine of the the second voice is the voice of Artan Grubi, the interpreter. The third voice is that of the accused, Mr. Beqa Beqaj, and again, the final voice is Mr. Artan Grubi, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask these questions on subsequent clips but if you do hear anything that doesn't comport with your recollection of the event, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: "AG: Nothing else. "JS: Okay. You told us on Tuesday that you knew nobody that is a witness or who was ever expressed their willingness to testify at the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: The accused here was asked a specific question. At any point in this interview or in fact the previous interview did he offer an answer that was different than this denial of knowing anyone who expressed a willingness to testify at the trial?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: It remained the same pretty much throughout. It was a series of denials.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: We are going to show another clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: Which is -- was a Wednesday last week. You had a conversation with somebody who used the name Salih Bajrami. "BB: Myself, no. "JS: Well, who also used the name Dull. "BB: Myself, not, I haven't."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did you understand the question you asked and the answer that the accused gave there?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did he at any point in the interviews change his answer regarding not having spoken to Salih Bajrami?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I couldn't say, but certainly on that occasion, he denied it and from the information that I had with me at that time, the reason for the question was that I had good reason to believe that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And if I can direct the Chamber to -- I believe there should be a hard copy in the trial exhibit folder. This part of the conversation is on page 10 and 11, and if I can read what it says starting at the top of page 11. "AG" -- who is the translator: "Myself not, I have not spoken. I guarantee that I have not spoken." "JS" -- Jonathan Sutch, the investigator: "You've never spoken to somebody called Salih Bajrami? "AG," answering for Beqa Beqaj: "What to say? I am saying no. Now, I have not spoken." That was a follow-up to the clip that we played; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: "JS: Telephone to anybody called Demir Limaj? "AG: If you believe me, I have never spoken and I have never known him and I don't --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sutch, do you know who Demir Limaj is? Did you learn that information through the course of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He's direct related to another accused, Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: How do you refer to Isak Musliu? What name do you refer to him by? "AG: Isak. "JS: Isak. You'd never called him Qerqiz? "AG: Never. "JS: You've never referred to him that way? "AG: I've never referred to him, because when he was arrested, I was in Slovenia, and I did not know --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: So in this question you've asked him about a pseudonym for Isak Musliu, Qerqiz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did at any point he indicate that he knew Qerqiz was the nickname?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I believe later on in the interview he actually referred to Isak Musliu as Qerqiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And at that point, did he explain or offer up an explanation why he used Qerqiz instead of Isak?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, the initial explain was, I believe, because I'd used it. But then he went on to give a further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what that explanation was?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I'd have to refresh my memory, I'm afraid. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: Okay. Did -- on Wednesday, the 13th, did you receive a call from Isak Musliu? "AG: I could not know. "JS: Did you speak to him last week? "AG: No. "JS: You didn't speak to him at all last week? "AG: No, I --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sutch, why did you pose this particular question?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, because we had telephone intercepts indicating that he had spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And still he denied it in face of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: And still he denied it which -- well, as you can see there, somewhat took away from the flow of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: "JS: I very briefly want to ask you about Azem Seferi. Do you know that person? "AG: Yes, I know him."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: In the course of your investigation, did you learn that Azem Seferi is?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: He's not a name that featured that much within it so I couldn't -- I probably couldn't accurately tell you who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "AG: The first time I --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dominguez - could we redact this, please, Registrar - you have to be extremely careful here. Are we going to be moving into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Dominguez.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you, let's move forward with this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: In the afternoon of Wednesday the 13th of October, at about 2.00, a telephone conversation took place between the person who I believe to be you and Isak Musliu, and halfway through the conversation the phone was passed to Bashkim, who continued the conversation. Do you recall that? "AG: I do not."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sutch, it appears to me, just watching the flow of the question you've asked, you're asking a longer, more specific question where you actually wait and let the interpreter at the interview translate the bits and pieces. Had you changed the flow or structure of your interview at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: That same day early in the morning a conversation took place."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't mean to play that. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I did understand the question. To say the structure of the interview hadn't -- to say it had changed is probably not entirely correct but the point is with the accused was to ensure that he understood all the questions. There were a lot of questions being asked and the questions were dotting around from specific conversations which we had monitored for some period of time, and it was important that the accused was clear as to what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And this was page 33, this last clip of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Up to that point in time, had the accused answered affirmatively to any of your questions that you remember or given you a sense that he was actually now going to confirm what you were confronting him with? Or at this point, had he still generally denied the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: To my recollection, he was certainly more forthcoming in that second interview but up to that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. Let's proceed with the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "JS: That same day, earlier on in the morning, a conversation took place between somebody calling himself Dull and also calling himself Salih Bajrami. And during that conversation, the person who we say is you said -- during that conversation, the person who the Tribunal will say is you, informed the caller that somebody would not be testifying. "AG: I never am. "JS: You're saying that's not you? "AG: No. "JS: And it's not you because you were at work without the telephone? Is that what you're saying? "AG: I am saying that no, I haven't spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "AG: No. "JS: Or Salih Bajrami.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Same question, Mr. Sutch. What was the set of facts related to there? Was it something that you had known about before you asked him?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Again, yes, but that's based on -- based on the telephone intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: "JS: Do you know that? Do you know that for a fact? Has he told you? Are you aware that he -- he is a witness for the Prosecution? "JS: Do you know that? Do you know that for a fact? Has he told you -- are you aware that he is a witness for the Prosecution? "AG: He is, but I'm not interested in that. "JS: So you do know that he is a witness? "AG: Everyone knows that."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Using a pseudonym -- it appears this clip doesn't mention the name but if you can use a pseudonym, do you remember which witness you were asking him about?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: At that point, it would have been B1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session for the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Let me ask you at the very beginning, it was a long bit and I apologise I don't have a copy for you to show you where I am but you said that, "we didn't ask to interview you about this because we didn't have any information. We didn't select your name out of many. We came directly to you because we -- we initially had information." This is before you actually posed the question. So what are you doing at that point?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, I'm informing him, and this is how the interview went, that -- that we had come to him because we had very specific information. So we went to a very specific individual. Everything wasn't [sic] said to -- to the accused at the beginning of the interview for the sake of completeness to ensure that every element of what we knew was put to him and he was given the opportunity to respond to it. This is one element of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: So when you're asking him this in the middle of the interview, is it in response to his general not answering any of your questions in the affirmative and you're explaining to him, we picked you out much not just at random but we picked you because we have specific information?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And at this point, he does admit to speaking with B1.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, he does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Is that the first point that you can recall him admitting that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: And in that clip, it mentioned that B1 -- he answered, "B1 called me once." At that point in time, you had reviewed transcripts of the wire-taps. (redacted) (redacted) B1 had only called him once?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, that wasn't accurate, no. And that really is how the interview progressed. The more information that was given -- the more information that was given, the more the accused would start to make certain admissions, although limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Can we go back into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dominguez, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: "JS: I have a couple of questions here. One, earlier on, you told us that you didn't know Isak Musliu as Qerqiz. And you just referred to him as Qerqiz. "AG: When I heard you, it just slipped my mouth. "JS: We have We didn't refer to Isak Musliu as Qerqiz, we referred to Qerqiz and Celiku. "AG: I slipped my tongue, because every word is repeated from the translator. And I've heard that he's called Qerqiz. Is there any problem with that?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did he offer up any explanation further than that?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I don't believe he did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, we will have to go back into private session for the next clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Dominguez.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "AG: I said --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: This is a short little clip here. Can you explain what was the context behind this? And if you need to refer to the transcript, I can play a little more. Only if you need to.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Again, this is a continuation of the conversation with B1, and the accused's recollection of what was said to B1. Again, on behalf, apparently on behalf of representatives of the -- of the accused in the Limaj trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: One more media clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: "PH: But you are also telling him that you will come and meet him with Fatmir Limaj's brother wherever he likes to meet you, just come and say that you have nothing to do with Fatmir Limaj and Isak. "AH: When he asked do I dare, can I come, I told him freely I can get out and meet you wherever. I do not have anything else --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: What is the significance of this?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Again, the significance is, from our understanding of the conversation here, that the accused is actually directly involved in the logistical process of ensuring or securing the attendance of the witness in Kosovo where he can be spoken to, again, by representatives of the other accused. And that he's taking an active role.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: I have one final clip and I think we should go into private session for it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van der Spoel, I give you the floor. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sutch, you met my client for the first time on the 19th of October last year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: You just testified that my client on that day said that he had just spoken to one witness; is that right? For the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We are in open session and I would like to remind you that you should proceed very cautiously and ensure -- make sure that you do not reveal the identity of protected witnesses. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Yes, Your Honour. I shall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MR. VAN DER SPOEL:

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: My question was that you just testified that my client said he had just spoken to one witness. You don't have to mention the name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, just to clarify, when I say -- when you say just spoken to one witness, that is that he had only spoken to one witness as opposed to he -- in the -- in the near past had spoken to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Were that his exact words?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: His exact words, I didn't record. I interrupted him. I made a note of what he had said in a statement which I believe has been submitted to the Court. Yeah, he said he had spoken to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Did he mention to you in what trial that person would be a witness?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No. The name wasn't mentioned but I had in the introductions I'd said my reasons for being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And they were?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: That I was speaking to -- I was coming to speak to him as a result of information that had been received concerning him and his contact with witnesses in the Fatmir Limaj trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And how many witnesses, without mentioning names, were involved in that trial?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact figure of -- for the witnesses involved in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: What information did you have before you interviewed my client concerning the suspicion against him?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: On the first occasion that he was interviewed, I had pretty much all the information that I had for the second interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: That was copies of the transcripts in relation to the telephone intercepts, as well as reports that had been completed by my colleague, Howard Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And those reports from Howard Tucker, did they concern my client, Mr. Beqa Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes, they did, yes. In part, not in whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And in part, what part?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Generally, in relation to his contact with B1 and B2 as referred to in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's concentrate on B1. What was the exact information you had from Howard Tucker concerning my client?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, the combination of the reports from Howard Tucker and of course the intercepts which would have been referred to within those reports, was that contact had been made between the two individuals and within that contact, the nature of the conversations was, as we allege, tantamount to interference with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's your conclusion. But if we look at the material, at the evidence, during examination-in-chief, actually, you were only interviewed about the interceptions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: So my question is still what other information did you have concerning my client and his involvement with witness B1?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Again, in order to have a full understanding of the witness himself, there was information contained within the reports concerning your client's relationship with people within the Fatmir Limaj trial, the accused and people working for the accused, as well as the relationship that your client has with -- with that particular witness, B1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that, please, be more specific, what the information was? It's very general what you're telling me now.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, it was very general. The most specific element of the information that we had in relation to the accused was the telephone intercepts. That's what everything was based upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Have you ever spoken to or met Witness B1?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No, I've never spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement with the telephone conversations B1 had with my client?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: No direct involvement. Essentially the process is an electronic process. There is not that much human involvement in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Those were my questions. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Prosecution have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: I would like to follow up on the questions regarding the information that Jonathan Sutch had from Howard Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically the documents regarding Howard Tucker's reports that you had in your possession?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: In general, yes; specifically, no. I would need to see the documents in order to refresh my memory on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to refresh the witness's memory by presenting material that we've previously disclosed to Defence and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document which has been provided by the witness, is it? Has the witness read this document? Does he know what it contains?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: This is a document that was provided and written by investigator Howard Tucker and I believe it was presented to the witness, and I can ask him those questions once I have a chance to give it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van der Spoel, do you have no objection to this? MR. VAN DER SPOEL: No, no objections at all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Have you had a chance now to review this document?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Please look specifically at page 2 and then after you've had a chance to look at it, let me know if this does refresh your recollection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please tell us what the content of the investigator's report you received from Howard Tucker was.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Essentially this -- it goes through the chronology from B1's perspective. And this particular document deals with conversations between the accused and B1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: When does the chronology begin? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: September 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: So this is approximately a month and a half before the interviews with the accused?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: This is prior -- prior to the interviews with the accused and also immediately prior to the -- to the start of the telephone intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Did the report indicate the nature of the call that caused B1 to inform the ICTY that there were things happening?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly suggested that -- there was inappropriate contact with witnesses in that particular trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Can you specify what the contact was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point can we go into private session because there will be family names mentioned, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open sessions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: The calls you referred to, you said there were multiple calls but not quite double digits. Are you referring to calls not just between the accused and B1 but also between other parties?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yeah. Calls made during the telephone intercepts. There were a number of calls made. There were some totally insignificant calls which were never -- the normal calls that people would make on a telephone which have absolutely nothing to do with the matters before the Court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dominguez. Mr. van der Spoel, the redacted parts in these documents lead to any questions? MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask you one short question. And this concerns the way you interpret Mr. Beqaj's words or what he ascertained to B1 when he said that if he took the decision to come, he must feel safe, and he will make quite sure that he will watch over that himself. How did you interpret Mr. Beqaj's words here? Do you understand it to be that he was guaranteeing his safety and that he was perhaps involved with other people who may have adversely affected B1's safety? The conclusion you drew in your evidence is based on what? Is it a personal impression? Is this a way you understand the entire situation? Or did you base this on a number of material facts?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've only been back in The Hague since January of this year, prior to which I spent four and a half years permanently assigned as part of the ICTY in Kosovo. So my knowledge of Kosovo is, whilst not being a citizen of Kosovo, I've lived and worked there for the last four and a half years. My understanding was this: That the accused had had direct contact with an indictee who was currently in the detention facility in Scheveningen. The nature of that conversation was that the accused should speak to a protected witness in his trial. Now, I was aware that there had been two, as I previously mentioned, unsuccessful attempts on that individual's life, and it was our prime concern that there shouldn't be a further, successful attempt. The fact that the accused had made contact with this person, and knowing who the accused was in the detention facility, being related by marriage to that person, was sufficient, in my mind, to suggest that guarantees made to B1 were intended to ensure his attendance in Kosovo. For what purpose, it's not really for me to speculate. But certainly, it was to make contact with representatives of the accused in the detention facility in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the words that were spoken, were they real guarantees or was it just to reassure the person concerned?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment. It's really the perception of the individual that hears the words -- heard the words from the accused. But the accused certainly hadn't been back to Kosovo for some time. I think it's true to say that the -- sorry, the witness hadn't been back to Kosovo for some time. I think it's fair to say the witness would be able to make contact with other people within Kosovo and establish what the potential security situation was like for him or potentially would be like for him. The fact of the matter was, though, that this was the person making these attempts. So in my mind, I was satisfied that the accused being the best apparently the best person to act as interlocutor between the accused in the detention facility and the witness, the relocated protected witness, he was making best efforts. Whether he could go through with his guarantees, I'm not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, this is a personal feeling of yours which is based on your general impression of the situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to thank you for coming here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to testify. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: May I follow up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: The Chamber has inquired on the power of the accused to guarantee B1's safety if he were to return to Kosovo or along those lines. In this trial, we've focused mostly on the wire-taps and the two witnesses, B1 and B2. We haven't brought in much testimony regarding the accused Isak Musliu except in the form of the transcripts from the Limaj case that are brought in under Rule 92 bis. Now, he's also asked in relation to Isak Musliu, who is the accused who has contacted -- I'm sorry, the Limaj accused who has contacted the accused in this case. Can you briefly explain, based on your being in Kosovo, Isak Musliu's position in Kosovo now in terms of his power and his military background, and also relate it to what happened in the Limaj case, what's been alleged against Isak Musliu, in terms of what power Isak Musliu may have if B1 were to go back to Kosovo and what the accused could actually do to protect him. In other words, who has the power in the situation, the accused or Isak? Also, if it's helpful, mention Fatmir Limaj and his power in Kosovo and his political and/or military position.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Specifically with Isak Musliu, to start off with, he held a command position within the Kosovo Liberation Army. Very briefly, the circumstances surrounding the indictment against him concern his involvement with a KLA detention facility and the treatment of detainees at that facility. The influence that he has in Kosovo is -- whilst may not -- obviously he's not in Kosovo himself, but there is an element of reputation that comes into play. He -- and by reputation, there is no reason to think that his wishes wouldn't be carried out from a remote location, his wishes in Kosovo wouldn't be carried out in a remote location. There is evidence to show that within the trials of former KLA members in Kosovo, that witnesses have been threatened, interfered with, and in cases been killed. I can go into detail, if you wish. My point here really is, though, that this is a very real threat, particularly in Kosovo, where the reputation of individuals who at one point in 1998, 1999, were -- held -- held the status of maybe national heroes, are being accused of crimes against civilians. Again, as I say, I could go into detail concerning -- concerning certain individuals and concerning witnesses who it's within my knowledge who have been threatened and in cases actually murdered because of their direct involvement with what are generally referred to as war crimes trials in the region of Kosovo. Fatmir Limaj, the co-accused of Isak Musliu, again held a political position within Kosovo, held a command position within the Kosovo Liberation Army prior to moving into politics, after the -- after the NATO entry in 1999. Again, there is no reason to believe that his wishes, should they be that somebody should interfere with witnesses identified to give evidence before the Tribunal in his case, there is no reason to believe that his wishes wouldn't be carried out even though he's not actually physically present there in Kosovo. Does that answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: That is half of the equation. So you've given us a little bit of background on Isak Musliu and Fatmir Limaj. In terms of the accused who you interviewed, did he indicate that he had any real power to protect B1? In fact, he does make some claims, I believe, in your interview, to being a person who works with his hands, who spent a lot of time in Slovenia out of the country, who doesn't have interest in this affair. He's a simple villager. Is that consistent?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I certainly -- to say that if we look at the financial aspect firstly, and to say that the accused would be in a position to pay for transport, the accused would be in a position to actually physically protect B1, I wouldn't for one minute believe that he was able to do that personally. However, knowing that, I would then -- I would then question why he was able to make those -- those assertions to B1, and that becomes a lot clearer when we subsequently discover through the intercepts that he is having direct communication with Isak Musliu in the detention facility. And having had any assurances made to him by Isak Musliu, it would then be a lot easier for him to make those -- pass on those assurances to any individual that happened to be -- that happened to have any concerns. I have no doubt that protection issues would be something within the power of the individuals, within the detention facility, through their representatives in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMINGUEZ
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dominguez. Mr. van der Spoel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Yes, one question concerning the question you asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: On the question of the Court, you said the following, that's page 45, line 9, "So in my mind, I was satisfied that the accused, being the best -- apparently the best person to act as interlocutor between the accused in the detention facility and the witness, the with relocated protected witness, he was making best efforts." So what is that based on? So in my mind, can you elaborate on that? Can we know something more what was going on in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: I do apologise here. The monitor wasn't on transcripts and I was going to try to follow what you were reading but I didn't follow what you were reading. So maybe if I could ask you just to repeat my quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Yes. I shall. "So in my mind I was satisfied that the accused, being the best -- apparently the best person to act as interlocutor between the accused in the detention facility and the witness, the relocated protected witness, he was making best efforts." So what went on in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Well, as you would have heard already, there is a loose relationship between -- or there is a relationship between the accused and B2 and there is a relationship between --

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: B2 or B1?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Between the accused and B2 and there is a relationship between B2 and B1. B1 -- there is also a relationship between Isak Musliu and the accused by marriage. The accused lives locally, not to B1 now but the accused lives locally to B2. And putting all of these relationships together, loose as some of them may be, the accused here is ideally placed. Whether or not the accused is the best person, I don't know. I don't know what's running through the minds of the individuals concerned in this process but certainly on the face of it, from the information that was -- that we with managed or that Mr. Tucker had managed to glean initially and combined with the telephone intercepts that had been -- that had been obtained later on, it seemed quite clear that this was a concerted effort to make -- to get B1 to come to Kosovo. Whether there were any other attempts made or not, I don't know. And certainly B1 doesn't know of any either. So we assume there are none.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: So you think that the combination, telephone interception and relationships are important, to get a whole view?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: The relationships between --

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: People.

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: Between people? They are important. They are important for a number of different reasons. Within Kosovo they are important because family relationships mean a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: And being that important, did you question B1 about the relationships and his view on the interceptions?

utterances.speaker: JONATHAN PETER SUTCH
utterances.text: As I've said before, I've never spoken to B1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN
utterances.text: Never spoken to B1. Thank you, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I think that we can finally release you and I would like to thank you for having testified here, for having taken the trouble to testify before this Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having said that, I think we can now deal with the issue of the exhibits. I believe that Defence counsel is not objecting to tendering the documents that the Prosecution wants to tender into evidence. Given the positions adopted by both parties, the Trial Chamber will admit these documents into evidence and the Registrar will provide each document with an exhibit number. If the Registrar is ready to proceed, we could deal with the matter right now. Or we could deal with it a little later. The Registrar has asked me whether the documents that will be tendered have to be under seal. You might want to consider your position, examine your position for the next hearing. Take your time, but I would just like to assure both parties that the documents have been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: There are certainly some exhibits that are going to need to be under seal. I would need a careful review to give you a breakdown. I wanted to just add one thing. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: One minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to proceed in the following manner. The Registrar and I believe the Court manager should establish a full list of the documents. They should be numbered, and the parts that have to be under seal, or redacted, should be clearly indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour. I just wanted to make sure that for -- for each exhibit, there should be an audio file, the English translation, and an Albanian translation. So there should be three parts to each. I don't know if that has been done in each case, but if it has, that's great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This isn't the first time. And the Registrar is quite used to dealing with such matters. The Registrar will now clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: How -- Your Honours how we had dealt with the matter for the MFI exhibits was that the original audio was given the P1 MFI and the translation in English was given P1 MFI E. And the Albanian was given 1A. So we have the original audio as the original number and then E for the English translation and A for the Albanian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Perfect. The only other issue, Your Honour, is that in the original exhibit list we had court orders for the covert measures for the interceptions. I withdrew them because there was a stipulation. I don't know if you want me to tender them for the record or not. I would ask for your advice on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not necessary. Defence counsel hasn't mentioned anything in this regard and I don't see why it would be necessary to tender this into evidence. I can see that Mr. van der Spoel is conferring [as interpreted] what I have just said. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: At this stage, the Prosecution would rest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I now have a question for Defence counsel. Is it your intention to file a motion pursuant to Rule 98 bis? MR. VAN DER SPOEL: No, it isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is another issue I would now like to raise. I would like to draw the parties' attention to Rule 86 which under(A) states the following: "After the presentation of all the evidence, the Prosecutor may present a closing argument. Whether or not the Prosecutor does so, the Defence may make a closing argument. The Prosecutor may present to a rebuttal argument to which the Defence may present a rejoinder." Under(B), the same rule, the following is stated: "Not later than five days prior to presenting a closing argument, a party shall file a final trial brief." And I'm now turning to the Defence. Will you content yourselves with the pleadings and the oral arguments or do you also intend to present written arguments, written submissions? MR. VAN DER SPOEL: We did, of course have a pre-trial meeting with Chambers and with the Prosecution. This is an exceptional case that not all the Rules will be applicable. That's why I was not intending on a 98 bis motion which I otherwise would have done within a normal proceedings. I was under the impression that we proceeded on the following, that there would be oral submissions as soon as possible -- of course first the Prosecutor's closing arguments, the Defence, and then the rest -- in a very short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: I will not file a final brief but I think some of our brief will be in writing. But not all of it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But at the same time -- because if this suits you, on Monday, the hearing could be used for the arguments, for the closing arguments, and for oral submissions. Would you agree to that? MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as far as the Prosecution is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We would like to make an oral submission, closing arguments, and if you would like a written submission, we'll be happy to do that. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Chamber will be satisfied with oral submissions, and I quite agree with the Defence's position when they say that this case should be completed as expeditiously as possible. And we should all do our best to ensure that a judgement is delivered very rapidly. Having said that, the next hearing will be held on Monday at 2.15 in the afternoon, in the same courtroom. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, May 2, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
